column1: In the EIA-267-A/ISO 841 CNC coordinate standard, which axis is always the principal spindle axis, and what defines its positive direction on a vertical mill?
column2: The Z-axis is always the principal spindle axis. On a vertical mill, positive Z is upward, away from the workpiece.

column1: Why does the right-hand-rule convention for X, Y, Z axes matter beyond simple labeling?
column2: It ensures the cross product of X and Y yields positive Z, keeping rotation matrices, angular corrections, and five-axis compensation algorithms mathematically consistent across all post-processors.

column1: What are the three components that must work in deterministic coordination for a CNC controller to always know the tool tip's position?
column2: 1) A physical system of linear/rotary guideways constraining motion to known axes, 2) a feedback system (encoders/resolvers) reporting actual position, 3) a logical mapping (work offsets/coordinate frames) tying position reports to a programmable coordinate frame.

column1: In G-code word-address format, what is the fundamental taxonomic distinction between G-codes and M-codes?
column2: G-codes (preparatory functions) control motion and machine state, while M-codes (miscellaneous functions) actuate machine peripherals — reflecting a physical division between motion/state control and peripheral actuation.

column1: What is 'modality' in G-code, and why is it architecturally important beyond saving keystrokes?
column2: Modality means most G-codes remain active until explicitly cancelled or superseded by another code in the same modal group. It is the mechanism by which the controller maintains a coherent internal state model (position, offsets, motion mode) across the entire program.

column1: State the Merchant equation relating shear plane angle (φ) to rake angle (α) and friction angle (λ).
According to the Merchant relationship, what is the effect of increasing rake angle on cutting forces and heat generation?
column2: A higher rake angle increases φ, thinning the shear zone, which reduces cutting forces and lowers heat generation.

column1: Why do inserts for interrupted cuts on hardened steel use highly negative rake angles despite the energy-efficiency cost?
column2: Negative rake suppresses the shear plane angle φ, thickening the deformation zone and dramatically increasing compressive stress at the edge, which protects the cutting edge from fracture during interrupted, high-impact cuts.

column1: What is the primary shear zone in metal cutting, and what causes the 'rhythmic' chip formation sometimes observed at high speed?
column2: The primary shear zone is a thin planar band inclined at angle φ where material fractures continuously ahead of the rake face and slides away as chip. The rhythmic eruption is caused by the shear plane angle oscillating as work-hardening temporarily arrests deformation before the material gives way again.

column1: Define accuracy versus repeatability in CNC precision specifications, and explain why a machine can have one without the other.
column2: Accuracy measures deviation between commanded and true absolute position; repeatability measures the machine's ability to return to the same location consistently. A machine can be highly repeatable (always returns to within 0.002 mm of a point) yet inaccurate (that point is systematically 0.050 mm off from nominal), because repeatability reflects consistency, not correctness relative to the true coordinate.

column1: What is the core failure mode of open-loop (stepper-based, no-encoder) CNC motion control under heavy cutting loads?
column2: Sudden increases in cutting force or aggressive acceleration can stall the motor or exceed pull-out torque, causing lost steps that accumulate as position error invisible to the controller (since there is no feedback loop to detect the discrepancy).

column1: Common misconception: G-code programming is just abstract numeric input to the controller. What is the first-principles correction to this view, per cutting mechanics theory?
column2: G-code and toolpath strategy are merely infrastructure; the machine only 'cares' about what happens at the tool tip in the contact zone, where kinetic energy converts to plastic deformation. Understanding this physical cutting-zone reality (shear zones, forces, heat) is essential to diagnosing issues like chatter, not just treating numbers as abstractions.
